chapters.title: Chapter 2: The One-Step and Multi-Step Binomial Tree

lessons.title: Building the One-Step Binomial Tree: Up, Down, and Risk-Neutral Probability

children.text: Chapter 1 built the core intuition using a one-step, two-state world described in plain rupee prices, a stock going to ₹120 or ₹90. That was deliberate, numbers you can check by hand build the right instincts fastest. From here on, this course switches to the standard notation every binomial tree textbook, paper, and trading system uses, u, d, and p, so that Lesson 3's jump to a multi-step tree is a small mechanical extension rather than a fresh derivation.
Standard Notation for a One-Step Tree

A stock at S0 today moves, over one step of length delta-t, to either S0 times u, the up state, or S0 times d, the down state, where u is greater than 1 and d is less than 1. A derivative on that stock, a call, a put, or anything else with a known payoff, is worth fu in the up state and fd in the down state. Chapter 2's job is finding f, its value today.

children.text: Chapter 1 discounted with a simple (1 + r) factor, easier to reason about for a first pass. Real derivatives pricing, Black-Scholes included, uses continuous compounding instead, growth over one step is e to the power r times delta-t, not (1 + r). It is the same discount factor already sitting inside the Black-Scholes formula from Lesson 1 of Chapter 1, and it is what every formula in this course uses from this point on.

body.latex: \text{Growth factor over one step} = e^{r\,\Delta t}, \qquad \text{Discount factor} = e^{-r\,\Delta t}
body.caption: The continuous-compounding convention this course uses from here forward.

children.text: The same replicating-portfolio argument from Chapter 1, Lesson 2 works here unchanged, only the symbols are general now instead of specific numbers. Solve for the risk-neutral probability p by requiring that, under it, the stock itself earns exactly the risk-free rate on average, and the result carries straight through to any derivative on that stock.

body.caption: The risk-neutral probability of an up-move, in general u, d, r, delta-t notation.
The one-step tree pricing formula. This single line, applied node by node, is the entire engine behind every tree this course builds.

children.text: A No-Arbitrage Condition That Must Hold

markDefs.definition: A probability value that falls outside the mathematically valid range of 0 to 1. In a binomial tree, this is a red flag that the chosen u, d, and r are inconsistent with no-arbitrage, not a number to plug in and continue with.

children.text: For p to be a genuine probability, it has to sit between 0 and 1, which forces the down factor, the risk-free growth factor, and the up factor into a strict order: d has to be less than e to the r delta-t, which in turn has to be less than u. If the risk-free growth factor sat above u, the stock's best possible outcome would still underperform a risk-free deposit, so shorting the stock and lending the proceeds would be a guaranteed profit, a genuine arbitrage. If it sat below d, the reverse trade would be the arbitrage. Getting a p outside 0 and 1 is not just an inconvenient number, it is the model flagging an
and, with it, a mispriced or inconsistent setup.
Worked Example: The Chapter 1 Setup, Formalized

body.text: Chapter 1, Lesson 2 priced this exact stock move, ₹100 to ₹120 or ₹90, with a ₹100-strike call, at ₹9.52 using simple (1 + r) compounding. This lesson's ₹9.59 is close but not identical, and that small gap comes entirely from the compounding convention, continuous versus simple, not from any change in the underlying logic. Same replicating portfolio, same no-arbitrage argument, marginally different arithmetic.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: For a one-step binomial tree to be free of arbitrage, which ordering must hold?
options: There is no restriction; any u, d, and r combination works
body.explanation: The risk-free growth factor has to sit strictly between the down and up factors. If it fell outside that range, either the stock or the risk-free asset would guarantee a better outcome than the other in every state of the world, which is exactly what an arbitrage-free market rules out.

body.title: Spotting a Broken Setup
body.scenario: A junior quant sets up a one-step tree with u = 1.02, d = 0.97, and an 8% continuously compounded risk-free rate over a 1-year step.
body.prompt: Compute the risk-neutral probability for this setup. What goes wrong, and what does it tell you about the inputs?
body.modelAnswer: The growth factor is e^0.08, about 1.0833, which already sits above u = 1.02. Plugging into the formula gives p = (1.0833 − 0.97) / (1.02 − 0.97) ≈ 2.27, a number nowhere near a valid probability between 0 and 1. This is exactly the no-arbitrage condition failing: the stock's best possible one-year outcome, a 2% rise, still underperforms an 8% risk-free deposit, so shorting the stock and lending the proceeds risklessly beats holding it in every single state. The fix is not mathematical, it is that the inputs themselves are inconsistent, either the up and down factors are far too narrow to represent a full year of real volatility, or the assumed rate is unrealistic for the horizon.

body.text: A one-step binomial tree is fully described by four numbers, u, d, r, and delta-t, plus one no-arbitrage condition, d less than e to the r delta-t less than u, that keeps the risk-neutral probability a genuine probability. Every multi-step tree in this course, starting next lesson, is this exact building block, repeated.

points: From this lesson forward, the course uses continuous compounding, e^(r × delta-t), the standard convention in real derivatives pricing and the same one already inside the Black-Scholes formula.
The risk-neutral probability of an up-move is p = (e^(r × delta-t) − d) / (u − d), derived from the identical replicating-portfolio logic built in Chapter 1.
The one-step pricing formula, f = e^(−r × delta-t) × [p × fu + (1 − p) × fd], is the entire computational engine behind every tree this course builds, applied once per node.
A valid tree requires d < e^(r × delta-t) < u. A probability outside 0 and 1 is not a number to use, it is a signal that the chosen inputs allow arbitrage.

Re-solving Chapter 1's worked example with continuous compounding gives ₹9.59 against the earlier ₹9.52, a small gap explained entirely by the compounding convention, confirming both chapters agree on the underlying economics.
